did_you_know.text: Did you know? The biblical word tsara'at does not necessarily mean the modern disease called leprosy; it refers to various skin conditions. The comparison to snow describes the hand’s white appearance.
Did you know? The word ye'or comes from Egyptian, and in the Bible it usually refers to the Nile. The Nile was central to water, agriculture, and daily life in ancient Egypt.

Did you know? The phrase “slow of speech and tongue” may describe difficulty speaking or expressing oneself, not necessarily a specific stutter. Moses presents his personal weakness just before his great mission.
Did you know? Aaron is portrayed as a brother who welcomes Moses with joy, without jealousy or rivalry. It offers an important idea about cooperation between brothers and between leaders.

Did you know? When Aaron is called Moses’ “mouth” and Moses is called “as God” to him, this does not mean that Moses becomes divine. It is a figurative description of Moses as the authority and Aaron as his spokesman.

Did you know? The title “My firstborn son, Israel” refers to the entire people of Israel, not to one individual. In the ancient Near East, the firstborn symbolized status, responsibility, and special rights within the family.
Did you know? A tzur is a flint stone, a hard material that can produce a sharp edge. In ancient times, people used flint for cutting tools even after they learned to work with metals.

Did you know? Horeb is the name of the mountain where Moses and Aaron met. Exodus also uses the name Sinai, so interpreters and scholars have discussed whether the two names refer to the same mountain or to different places.

Did you know? In the Bible, “elders” are not simply elderly people; they are also community leaders and representatives. Councils of elders were a common way to organize communities and make decisions.
Did you know? The phrase “they bowed and worshiped” uses two related verbs to emphasize deep respect. In the Bible, bodily gestures often express gratitude and faith as well.
